questions.q: Define situational irony and give a one-sentence example from daily life (not from the textbook).
questions.a: Situational irony occurs when the outcome of a situation is the opposite of what was expected or intended. Example: A fire station burns down. A wrong answer (e.g., "irony is when something funny happens") reveals the student confuses irony with humor or coincidence, missing the core "expectation vs. reality" structure.

questions.q: In the story, the writer says, "viw osQ lkFk <kbZ lky" (the small line with the pen). Explain in your own words why this statement is ironic, considering the writer's profession.
questions.a: The writer is a professional author (fI+kQYedkj) whose livelihood depends on writing, yet he cannot produce even a single line because his pen fails. The irony lies in the gap between his identity (a writer) and his immediate reality (unable to write). A wrong answer focusing only on the pen's mechanical fault shows the student misses the professional-personal contrast that creates the irony.

questions.q: Identify one object in the story (other than the pen) that functions as a symbol. State what it literally is and what abstract idea it represents.
questions.a: The doll (oqQÙkk) given to the child (Hkwyks) is literally a toy, but it symbolizes the writer's own creative work—fragile, crafted, and vulnerable to external judgment. A wrong answer naming the pen again shows the student cannot transfer the symbol-identification skill to a new object; an answer giving only the literal meaning misses the abstract layer.

questions.q: Compare the irony in the pen-failure episode (opening) with the irony in the doll episode (middle). How does the *type* of irony shift, and what does this shift reveal about the writer's evolving conflict?
questions.a: The opening uses situational irony (tool fails the professional). The doll episode introduces dramatic irony: the writer and reader know the doll is a cheap replacement, but the child (Hkwyks) treats it as precious. The shift moves the conflict from external (mechanical failure) to internal (artistic insecurity—fear his work is a "fake"). A wrong answer listing both as "situational" shows inability to distinguish irony types; missing the "internal conflict" link shows lack of thematic synthesis.

questions.q: Critique this student statement: "The pen is a symbol of writing, so the whole story is just about writing." Is this a sufficient symbolic reading? Justify.
questions.a: No, it is reductive. The pen symbolizes not just "writing" but the *struggle for authentic expression*—its failure mirrors the writer's block; its eventual working mirrors breakthrough. The doll, the storm (ckfj'k), and the historical portraits (tosYV, pfpZy, etc.) expand the symbolism to legacy, fear, and political context. A "sufficient" judgment reveals the student treats symbols as simple one-to-one codes rather than multi-layered thematic nodes.

questions.q: Write a 4-line micro-story that uses *both* situational irony and a symbol (choose any object) to convey the theme "unexpected help."
questions.a: Example: "The lighthouse keeper forgot to light the lamp. A ship crashed. The wreckage washed up—dry firewood for his cold hearth. The lamp (symbol of guidance) failed; the disaster (symbol of chaos) saved him." A poor answer uses only irony or only symbolism, or makes the symbol explicit ("the lamp symbolized hope") instead of letting the object carry the meaning implicitly.
